<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README content, this project is a Go-based “Cursor Free Trial Reset Tool” – a command-line utility that resets or “modifies” key identifiers (machine IDs, MAC addresses, etc.) in Cursor’s configuration files (and even the Windows Registry) to bypass trial restrictions. The tool supports multiple operating systems (Windows, macOS, Linux) and is structured to allow safe, automated, and even interactive use.

Below is a step-by-step guideline for drawing a detailed and accurate system design/architecture diagram tailored specifically for this project.

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Command Entry Point (CLI): The primary executable is located in cmd/cursor-id-modifier. This is where program execution starts.
   • Internal Modules:
     – Config Module (internal/config/config.go): Loads and manages configuration data (i.e., file paths for Cursor’s “storage.json”, etc.).
     – Language Module (internal/lang/lang.go): Manages any message strings or localization.
     – Process Manager (internal/process/manager.go): Handles adjustments of running Cursor processes, ensuring safe termination before modifications.
     – UI Module (internal/ui): Contains code for displaying logos, spinners, and other terminal UI elements to enhance interactivity.
   • Utility Package:
     – ID Generation (pkg/idgen/generator.go): Generates new unique identifiers used for aspects like telemetry or machine ID fields.
   • Scripts & Automation:
     – The scripts directory holds batch/shell/PowerShell scripts to build, install, or run the tool on different systems. Also included are CI/CD workflows under .github/workflows and build configurations (e.g., .goreleaser.yml).

2. Determine the Relationships and Interactions:
   • The CLI (main.go) calls into internal modules (config, process, ui, lang) and utility packages (pkg/idgen) to orchestrate the tool’s behavior.
   • The config module reads/writes to external configuration files (e.g., storage.json) and, on Windows, prompts for registry modifications.
   • The process manager ensures safety by checking and terminating running Cursor processes before changes.
   • The UI components provide feedback (spinners, logos) during execution.
   • The scripts interact externally as wrappers that trigger the primary Go executable in a system-specific way (e.g., via curl pipelines in one-click install commands).

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modularity: The structure separates CLI (cmd/) from internal core logic (internal/) and utility functions (pkg/). This modular design isolates concerns such as configuration management, process handling, and user interface.
   • Platform-Specific Handling: Different scripts and parts of internal logic ensure functionality across Windows, macOS, and Linux (e.g., registry modifications on Windows versus file system touches on macOS/Linux).
   • Safety & Atomicity: The design includes features like process checks, backups before registry or configuration file modifications, and error handling with safe file operations.
   
4. Include Relevant Technologies & External Dependencies:
   • Programming Language: Go (indicated via go.mod/go.sum and source code in main.go).
   • CI/CD: GitHub Actions (workflows under .github/workflows) and GoReleaser for release automation (.goreleaser.yml).
   • Scripting: Shell/BAT/PowerShell scripts under scripts/ for easing cross-platform installation and execution.
   • External Tools: Used for modifying system settings such as Windows Registry or network configurations on macOS/Linux—requiring admin privileges.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • Given this is a cross-platform CLI tool, emphasize the division between the core application logic (internal packages) and the platform-specific scripts/installers.
   • Clearly delineate the flow starting from the CLI entry point and map out how internal modules interact (e.g., CLI → [config, process, ui, lang] → pkg/idgen).
   • Illustrate external integrations: How the tool interfaces with system configuration files, the Windows Registry, and process management.
   • Reflect CI/CD and build/deployment facets to show how automated builds trigger releases.

6. Elements to be Included in the Diagram:
   • A box labeled “CLI Application” (cmd/cursor-id-modifier) that serves as the entry point.
   • Internal module boxes:
     - Config Manager (internal/config)
     - Language Helper (internal/lang)
     - Process Manager (internal/process)
     - UI Components (internal/ui)
   • Utility Package box: ID Generator (pkg/idgen)
   • Arrows showing invocation flow: the CLI calls these modules to perform tasks.
   • Annotations indicating external dependencies:
     - Interaction with system’s configuration file (storage.json, registry)
     - Scripts and deployment pipelines (under scripts/ and .github/workflows)
   • Differentiation using color coding or different shapes:
     - e.g., blue boxes for internal Go modules, green for utility libraries, yellow for external system integrations, and red for scripts that require elevated permissions.

7. Detailed Diagram Construction Approach:
   • Start at the top with the “User / CLI Invocation” node.
   • Add an arrow to “CLI Application (cmd/cursor-id-modifier/main.go)”.
   • Branch from the CLI to several components:
        · Internal Config (reads/writes storage files and registry entries)
        · Process Manager (safely terminates and handles running Cursor processes)
        · UI Module (displays logos/spinner for progress feedback)
        · Lang Module (handles messaging)
        · ID Generation (provides new identifier values)
   • Draw directional arrows from these modules back to the CLI where results are displayed to the user.
   • On the side, indicate “External Integration” with OS services (file system access, Windows Registry modification, network scripts for remote execution), connected to appropriate modules.
   • Optionally, include a lower section for “Auxiliary Scripts & CI/CD” linking GitHub workflows, build scripts, and one-click installation workflows that eventually trigger the main executable.

By following these guidelines, you will produce a comprehensive system design diagram that accurately reflects the tool’s architectural components and their interactions. This detailed diagram will serve as an excellent reference for both understanding and extending the project.
</explanation>
